code generation, debugging, reviews and memory use must respect this constraint even

 ## Search results
GRU4Rec’s BPR-max directly addresses weak discrimination among high-scoring negatives: softmax weights over negative scores emphasize difficult competitors, avoiding gradient dilution from averaging many easy BPR pairs. Its objective is −log Σj[softmax(r−)j σ(r+−r−j)], with optional negative-score regularization. The authors’ implementation recommends BPR-max or cross-entropy. This remains the strongest family-specific starting point, although the underlying work predates 2023. [GRU4Rec paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)

Recent research supports controlled hardness rather than indiscriminately choosing the hardest items. A 2023 analysis connects hard-negative BPR to partial AUC and top-K ranking, with hardness requiring dataset-specific tuning. Hard-BPR (2024) modifies the objective to reduce false-negative damage under dynamic sampling. Neither establishes gains on this pinned Amazon benchmark. A 2025 sampled-softmax paper also identifies a logQ subtlety: the positive is always included, unlike sampled negatives, so applying the same correction indiscriminately leaves bias. [Hard-negative theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03472), [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276), [LogQ correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)

Experiment implication: compare BPR-max, sampled cross-entropy with correction matched to the actual sampling process, and Hard-BPR as separate single-GRU4Rec trials. Exclude training-known positives from negative pools; tune moderate hardness before aggressive mining. Preserve one checkpoint per category and select exclusively by fixed four-category macro validation HR@10. Improved Electronics training margins alone would not establish better recommendation quality.

---

Recent work supports text-informed sequential recommendation, but the retrieved papers do not establish the exact combination of GRU4Rec, corpus-only text learning, and semantic hard negatives. [Recformer (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13731) represents items as attribute-text sentences and learns sequential retrieval through pretraining and finetuning; its Transformer backbone is outside this experiment’s family constraint. [JEPA4Rec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10512) learns item-text representations through masked representation prediction and reports benefits in low-resource settings, but likewise uses a Transformer and two-stage training. These are architectural inspiration, not direct evidence that a small text encoder trained from scratch will improve GRU4Rec.

A compatible experimental hypothesis: randomly initialized token embeddings, title/description pooling or a small CNN, and a learned projection jointly integrated with item-ID embeddings inside one GRU network. Shared lexical parameters could help sparse items express purpose, artist, franchise, or product relationships; this remains an inference requiring validation. For sampling, [GNNO (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10047) mines hard negatives through item-graph neighborhood overlap, demonstrating an interaction-derived alternative to external semantic models. [R2NS (2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) investigates negative recall and reranking for sequential recommendation. A conservative adaptation would mix random negatives with moderately similar title/description candidates, exclude known training positives, and tune hardness cautiously: similarity can identify plausible positives as well as useful negatives. Compare text integration and sampling separately using the fixed macro validation HR@10; retain one jointly trained GRU checkpoint per category.

---

The closest GRU-compatible result is [2Gated-TimeGRU, HICSS 2024](https://aisel.aisnet.org/hicss-57/da/data_science/10/). It incorporates intervals between consecutive interactions into a time-sensitive GRU architecture to capture short-term preferences and interest evolution. Authors report improved recommendation accuracy on real datasets; this supports testing explicit elapsed-time conditioning within the existing recurrent backbone. [FMRES, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104070) combines personalized forgetting curves, memory replay and GRU temporal modeling. Its full architecture requires social relationships and rating-derived information unavailable here; the transferable idea is jointly learned retention sensitive to elapsed time.

Practical experiment suggested by these findings, rather than a verified reproduction: condition GRU reset/update gates on transformed inter-event gaps, or apply learned positive-rate decay to the previous hidden state before the GRU update. Compare against the corrected baseline using macro validation HR@10; gains on this benchmark remain unproven. Learn decay jointly with item embeddings and recurrence in one network per category. Preserve hidden state across padding, calculate gaps only between real historical events, and read the final nonpadding position—never count−1 for left-padded histories. Use only timestamps available at prediction time; avoid dependence on the unknown next-interaction timestamp.
